definition: Disavow means to deny knowledge of, responsibility for, or association with something.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word disavow. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know disavow should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The candidate moved quickly to disavow the insulting flyer, insisting that no one on her staff had approved it.
To deny is the everyday act of saying something is not true, while to disavow is a more formal, public refusal to be connected with it.
To disavow is to deny any association, but to repudiate is even stronger, a complete and often dramatic rejection of the thing itself.

To disclaim is to state formally that you have no claim to or responsibility for something - companies disclaim liability in fine print. Disavow is more personal and pointed: a public figure disavows a statement or an ally to cut off any association with it. Disclaiming manages legal exposure; disavowing defends a reputation.

To renounce is to formally give up something you actually held - a title, a claim, a belief you once professed. To disavow is to deny that a connection exists at all, or to reject responsibility for it. You renounce what was yours; you disavow what you insist was never yours.

To reject is simply to refuse to accept something - an offer, an idea, an application - and it can be entirely private. To disavow is a public, on-the-record act: openly denying any association with the thing. You can reject a plan silently in your head; disavowing it requires an audience.
to admit or accept as true
to publicly support or approve

When a wellness blog claimed his sleep study proved that naps cure illness, Dr.
Ferro published a letter to disavow the claim.
He explained that his research had never tested anything of the kind, and he wanted no association with the exaggeration.
Ferro publicly denies any connection between himself and the blog's claim, which is exactly what it means to disavow something.
Formal / public statements
Disavow almost always describes a public, on-the-record denial, often by an official, an organization, or a public figure.
If you privately doubt something, you are merely skeptical; when you formally announce you have no part in it, you disavow it.

The trouble began when a viral ad promised that Meridian's sneakers could cure knee pain.
The clip looked official: the fonts matched, the logo gleamed, and within a day two million people had watched it.
Meridian's founder went on the morning shows to disavow the ad, stating plainly that no one at the company had made it, approved it, or paid for it.
She did not stop at a press release; she named the claim false on every channel the ad had reached.
Analysts noted the difference between quiet legal notices and what she chose: a public, personal denial of any connection to the promise.
